description: How to take product photos for AI with a phone, then try new settings, a batch of looks, and a listing image you can compare with the real item.
h1: How to Take Product Photos for AI With Just Your Phone
lead: To take product photos for AI, shoot the real item on your phone in window light, then place it in a new setting without a studio. Leave filters off so the later image still matches what you ship.
secondary_keywords: how to photograph products for an online store
summary: Shoot at product height in window light, with filters off and the label readable, then try a new setting from that same photo.

sections.h2: New settings from one phone photo
paras: Once the source photo is sharp, you can place the same item somewhere new. The product should still be the one you ship.
A coast or a bright outdoor table. Use it when the product is about sun, travel, or summer. Check that the color did not shift warm.
A dry, open setting. Sand, stone, or a pale wall. Good for a rugged item. Watch the shadows so the label stays readable.
A minimal table. A plain board, gray card, or bare wood. This is the safest listing look, and it is the right start if you are unsure.
An indoor room. A kitchen counter, a gym bench, a desk. Name the surface and the light in one sentence, such as "A matte black bottle on a gym bench in early light."

sections.h2: Reasons to make the photo here
paras: You already did the hard part with your phone. The rest replaces the studio day, not the truth of the product.

A smaller bill than a shoot. You are not hiring a set, a stylist, or a model for every color. One image is 24 credits, and that cost shows before the job starts. Starter is $24.50 a month for 200 credits, Pro is $35 for 300, and Premium is $63 for 600.
No waiting on a booking. A usable listing image comes back from a photo you took today. You still compare it with the real item before you publish.

A batch when the catalog is long. Make several shots from one photo. Each image is its own 24-credit job. A failed job returns the credits. A developer can start those jobs through the API from your shop system.

No model hire, unless you want a person. Skip props you do not own. If you do want someone holding the item, pick a generated presenter and do not call them a customer. There is an [actor library](page:ai-actors) when the picture needs a person.
Start when the shop is quiet. A Sunday night is fine. Each job still costs 24 credits. There is no free plan.
Try two backgrounds before you pick a listing. A plain table and a room, or two crops, then run the winners as separate ads. That is a test, not a promise about the return.

sections.h2: How to make the product photo in 3 steps
paras: Get the phone photo right, choose the look, then check the result against the real item.
Describe it, or upload it. Use the regular camera and keep the whole product sharp.
Rest the phone on books or a small tripod. Use the volume button or a two-second timer.
Fill most of the frame and leave a slim margin. Step closer instead of pinching to zoom.
Set the product beside a window in bright, indirect daylight. Turn the ceiling lights off.
If sun hits the table, tape baking paper or a thin white sheet over the glass.
Warm bulbs mixed with daylight shift the color, and that shift follows into later images.
A plain board, gray card, or bare wood top is enough background.
Wipe dust, peel stickers, and smooth anything soft before you shoot.
Hold the phone level with the product, and keep every edge inside the frame.
Switch portrait mode, filters, and beauty settings off. They change the edges and the color.
Shooting down on a bottle or a box makes it look as if it is tipping backward.
Tap the label to lock focus. If whites blow out, lower the brightness until texture returns.
Take a straight front, then two or three more sides while the setup is still out.
A mug wants the handle, a look inside, and the mark on the base.
A shoe wants the profile, a three-quarter front, and the sole.
Lay clothing flat or hang it on a plain door, then add one close frame of the cloth.
Upload each side you care about. Do not ask the tool to invent a side it never saw.
Zoom until you can read the label. Compare the color with the real item in daylight.
Upload the original file, not a screenshot or a picture that passed through a chat app.
JPG, JPEG, PNG, WebP, HEIC, HEIF, BMP, TIF, and TIFF files all work, up to 32 MB.
Name the product, the surface, and the light in one plain sentence. Leave prices out.
Pick the look before it runs: outdoor table, dry background, minimal surface, or a room.
A beach scene and a plain table are two choices. You are aiming the picture, not hoping.
When the image comes back, hold the real item beside the screen.
Check the color, the label, and the shape. Fix it with a follow-up sentence if needed.
Add the price later in your own editor, where the spelling stays yours.
Open [lifestyle photos](page:lifestyle-photos), [change the background](page:change-background), or a [white background](page:white-background).
The same still can start [AI image to video](page:image-to-video) when the listing also needs a clip.

sections.h2: Examples of the photos you can make
paras: Same item, different rooms. None of these should invent a detail the source photo did not contain.
A sunscreen tube on a bright outdoor table, label forward, with the shade left alone.
A bottle on a gym bench in early light, cap and label both readable.
A shoe in profile, from a photo that actually showed that side.
The same shoe from a three-quarter front, then the sole, each from its own source photo.
A mug with the handle visible, on a bare wood top, room kept simple behind it.
A candle on wood, wick and label both inside the frame.
A necklace on a dark top, clasp visible, no invented chain length.
A snack bag standing up, every edge inside the frame.
Headphones on a desk, both cups visible if the source photo had them.
A serum bottle with the dropper on, shade checked against the real bottle.
A tote laid flat, handles spread, filters left off.
A small appliance from the front, cord included only if the source photo showed it.

faq.q: What does this product photo tool do?
faq.a: It makes a new product image from a photo you already took and a plain sentence about the setting. You still shoot the real item so the label, the color, and the shape stay honest.

You upload a sharp phone photo and say where the product should sit. The new image follows that photo. Hold the real item next to the screen and check the color, the label, and the shape before you list it.

faq.q: What should I look for in the result?
faq.a: The product should match the item you ship, the cost should show before the job starts, and a failed job should return the credits. One image is 24 credits. If the label is wrong, do not publish that file.

No. There is no free plan. One image is 24 credits. Starter is $24.50 a month for 200 credits, Pro is $35 for 300, and Premium is $63 for 600. Downloads have no watermark. See [pricing](page:pricing).

faq.q: Are these photos useful for a shop?
faq.a: Yes, for listings, catalogs, and ads, as long as you compare them with the real item. A plain background is enough to start. Make a white version later if a marketplace asks for one.

faq.q: What do I gain by doing it this way?
faq.a: A listing image without a studio booking, more than one setting from the same photo, and a file you can use in the shop. You can also send the still into a short video. Each job shows its credit cost first.

faq.q: Can I use the photos in my shop and in ads?
faq.a: Yes. Downloaded photos are yours to use in listings and ads, and they do not include a watermark. You still need the right to the product photo you uploaded. Leave other brands' logos and famous people out of the frame.
